title: Environmental gentrification

definition.text: A process in which cleaning up pollution or adding green amenities raises local property values and draws wealthier residents into a formerly polluted or neglected neighbourhood.

facts.text: Green amenities include parks, green roofs, gardens and green, energy-efficient building materials.
Greening can displace low-income households physically through rising housing costs, and can also displace long-time residents culturally, socially and politically.
The term was first coined by Sieg and colleagues in 2004 and combines the older topics of gentrification and environmental justice.
Green spaces tend to raise housing prices when housing supply is too small to meet local or regional demand.
Property prices near New York's High Line rose by 35%, and near Chicago's Bloomingdale Trail by 13.8% to 48.2%.
After Superfund cleanups, wealthier and more educated newcomers tend to move in while earlier residents are slowly priced out.
Cooling measures against the urban heat island, such as green walls and green roofs, can also trigger higher prices and displacement.

notes: The exact definition is called a topic of debate (909f41200566), but only as a hedge; not marked contested.

title: Environmental personhood

definition.text: A legal idea that gives certain natural entities, such as rivers or forests, the status of a legal person.

facts.text: Legal personhood gives the entity rights, protections, responsibilities and legal liability; because a river cannot go to court, a guardian acts on its behalf.
A legal person cannot be owned, so no one can own an entity that has been given legal personality.
Christopher D. Stone first proposed legal personality for natural objects in the 1970s in his article "Should trees have standing?"
New Zealand declared Te Urewera a legal entity in 2014 and the Whanganui River a legal person in 2017, represented by one guardian from the iwi and one from the Crown.
An Indian state High Court gave the Ganges and Yamuna legal-entity status in March 2017, but sceptics noted that the declaration alone would not stop their pollution.
In 2022 Spain recognised the Mar Menor lagoon and its basin as a legal person, the first ecosystem in Europe with its own rights.
Supporters say it lets people sue to protect nature without showing harm to humans, and honours Indigenous relationships with the land.
Critics note that a legal person can also be sued, raising questions about who is liable for harms such as natural disasters.

contested_note: The idea is controversial even among environmentalists, some of whom back rights of nature but not personhood as the way to secure them.
